title: A New Class of Cancer Drugs Delivers Radiation Directly to Tumours. ASCO 2026 Data Suggests It Could Replace Chemotherapy for Some Patients.
excerpt: Radioligand therapies attach radioactive atoms to molecules that seek out cancer cells. The latest results against prostate cancer are the strongest yet — and the field now commands 40 per cent of Novartis's oncology R&D budget.
body:
For decades, cancer treatment has followed a familiar playbook: surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy. Each generation of drugs has been more targeted than the last, but all share a basic limitation — they cannot reliably distinguish cancer cells from healthy ones without significant collateral damage.

A new class of therapies presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) annual meeting in Chicago is challenging that paradigm in a way that could matter deeply to South Asian families.

What Radioligand Therapy Actually Does

Radioligand therapy (RLT) works by attaching a radioactive atom — typically lutetium-177 or, in the newest generation, actinium-225 — to a molecule engineered to seek out a specific protein on cancer cells. The molecule finds its target, binds to it, and delivers a lethal dose of radiation to the tumour from the inside. Healthy tissue is largely spared.

Think of it as a guided missile compared to the carpet bombing of traditional chemotherapy.

Novartis, the Swiss pharmaceutical giant that has become the largest player in this space, presented two sets of data at ASCO 2026 that underline how rapidly the field is advancing.

The Pluvicto Results: Moving Into Earlier Treatment

The first dataset came from the PSMAddition trial, which tested Novartis's existing drug Pluvicto (lutetium Lu 177 vipivotide tetraxetan) in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer — a much earlier stage than where the drug is currently approved. Among 1,144 patients, Pluvicto plus standard hormone therapy reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 28 per cent compared to hormone therapy alone.

The results were consistent across every subgroup tested: patients with high-volume disease, low-volume disease, newly diagnosed cases, and recurrent cancers. The hazard ratios ranged from 0.72 to 0.74 — a level of consistency rarely seen in oncology trials.

If approved for this earlier setting, Pluvicto could become part of first-line treatment for prostate cancer rather than a last resort.

The Actinium Breakthrough: Next-Generation Radiation

The second dataset was arguably more exciting. Novartis presented Phase 1 results for an experimental actinium-225-based drug — a next-generation radioligand that delivers a more potent form of radiation (alpha particles instead of beta particles) directly to cancer cells.

In a 101-patient study, 52.5 per cent of patients who had already been treated with Pluvicto saw their PSA levels — a key marker for prostate cancer — drop by at least half. Among patients with no prior radioligand treatment, the response rate exceeded 85 per cent.

"These are early data, but the signal is clear," said Novartis Chief Medical Officer Shreeram Aradhye, who noted that the company is moving ahead with two late-stage studies. Side effects, including dry mouth and severe anaemia, will need careful management.

Why This Matters for South Asian Families

Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in men worldwide, and South Asian men face a particular challenge. Research has consistently shown that while South Asian men are diagnosed at slightly lower rates than white men in Western countries, they tend to present with more aggressive disease and at later stages. Cultural stigma around discussing prostate health, lower screening rates, and a tendency to delay medical consultations all contribute to worse outcomes.

The rise of radioligand therapy offers a less toxic, more targeted alternative to chemotherapy — which is especially relevant for older patients who may not tolerate traditional treatment well.

A $10 Billion Industry Takes Shape

Radioligand therapies now account for nearly 40 per cent of Novartis's cancer R&D investments. Pluvicto and Lutathera, its two approved radioligand drugs, brought in a combined $2.8 billion last year.

The field has attracted virtually every major pharmaceutical company. Eli Lilly acquired Point Biopharma for $1.4 billion. Bristol Myers Squibb bought RayzeBio for $4.1 billion. AstraZeneca purchased Fusion Pharmaceuticals for $2.4 billion. Bayer continues to develop its own pipeline.

TD Cowen analysts called the Novartis actinium data "a clear efficacy signal" but cautioned that managing side effects would be crucial for broader adoption.

What to Watch

Two Phase 3 trials of the actinium-based drug are now underway. If they confirm the early results, the drug could reach the market within three to four years. Meanwhile, Pluvicto's expansion into earlier-stage prostate cancer could come sooner, with regulatory filings expected in 2027.

For South Asian families with a history of prostate cancer, the practical takeaway is straightforward: the treatment landscape is shifting in their favour, but early screening remains critical. The most targeted therapy in the world cannot help if the cancer is not detected in time.
nri_angle: South Asian men face higher rates of aggressive prostate cancer and tend to present at later stages due to lower screening rates and cultural stigma. Radioligand therapy's targeted, less toxic approach is especially relevant for this population, offering an alternative to chemotherapy with fewer side effects for older patients.
